To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
African American students are more likely to have parents who are less involved with their mathematics learning and participation than are other racial/ethnic groups.

(1) African American students are not doing as well in mathematics as they should, given the resources available to them; (2) African American students' mathematics achievement is not the result of low motivation or a lack of interest; and (3) African American students do not have a deficit of mathematics ability.
African American parents and community members believe that mathematics learning and doing are racialized experiences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that race and racism play in the construction of the social identities of African Americans.
how race and racial identity are conceptualized, and how these conceptualizations influence the experiences of African Americans.
the ways that race and racism are lived in the everyday lives of African Americans in this country. (Sellers et al. p. 19).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
race is a social and political construction, a social reality, that has had and continues to have real effects for the lives of African American people in the United States and around the world.
the African American experience is a racialized experience. (Sellers et al., 1998, pp. 19-20)

African Americans have experienced and continue to experience a history of racialized experiences in the U.S. society that are not shared by Whites, and that these experiences have shaped the lives of African American parents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
African Americans are a group of people who are defined by their racial group membership.
the African Americans' struggle for mathematics literacy is part of a larger struggle against racial subjugation and oppression.
African Americans are a group of people who have experienced a history of racial discrimination, and who continue to experience racial discrimination in the present. (Sellers et al., 1998, pp. 18-19)
The main takeaway from our work is that
mathematics learning and engagement is a racialized form of experience for African Americans.
African American parents' beliefs about mathematics learning and participation are shaped and constrained by a long history of oppression.
the struggle for mathematics literacy for African American parents and students must be conceptualized as part of a larger struggle for social and educational equity.
